title: Linear Neural Networks for Classification
oneLiner: Classification networks turn a weighted sum into probabilities: a sigmoid for yes/no, a softmax for one-of-many, trained by nudging weights after each small batch of examples.

what.html:
Classification predicts a category: spam or not, which digit, which disease. A linear classification network computes a score (a weighted sum of the features) and turns it into a probability.

Everyday versionA doctor adds up evidence (fever counts a lot, a cough a little) into a score, then translates the score into "how likely is flu?". High score → nearly certain; score around zero → 50/50. That translation is the sigmoid; with many possible illnesses, softmax shares 100% of belief among them.

For two classes it's logistic regression (one neuron + sigmoid); for K classes it's softmax regression (K neurons + softmax).

why.html:
• Most real decisions are categories: spam filters, medical tests, image labels, sentiment.
  • Plain linear regression can output −0.3 or 1.7, which aren't probabilities. We need outputs between 0 and 1.
  • These models are the output layer of nearly every deep classifier, so understanding them here pays off in every later module.

how.title: Three kinds of classification
how.html: Binary: two classes (spam / not spam). Multi-class: exactly one of K classes (digit 0–9). Multi-label: several labels can be true at once (a movie can be action and comedy). Binary models output P(class 1), and we predict class 1 when that's at least 0.5.

how.title: Squash the score with a sigmoid
how.html: The sigmoid σ(z) = 1/(1 + e⁻ᶻ) turns any score into a number between 0 and 1: big positive → near 1, big negative → near 0, zero → exactly 0.5. Its slope is σ(1 − σ), at most 0.25, which makes the maths of learning neat.

how.title: One neuron, one decision line
how.html: Inputs × weights, summed, then sigmoid. Since σ(z) ≥ 0.5 exactly when z ≥ 0, the boundary between the two predicted classes is where the weighted sum is zero: a straight line in 2-D (a flat "hyperplane" in more dimensions).

how.title: Measure surprise: cross-entropy
how.html: If the true answer is 1 and you said 0.9, the loss is small (0.1); if you said 0.01, the loss is huge (4.6). Cross-entropy = −log(probability you gave to the right answer). It punishes confident mistakes hard, comes from maximum likelihood, and gives a bowl-shaped loss for this model.

how.title: Learn from one example at a time (SGD)
how.html: Batch gradient descent looks at all the data before each step: accurate but slow. Stochastic gradient descent picks one random example, computes how wrong it was, and nudges the weights right away. The nudge is beautifully simple: (prediction − truth) × input. The path is noisy, but there are many more steps.

how.title: A worked example: passing an exam
how.html: Students who studied 1, 2, 3, 4 hours; the last two passed. Start with weights (0, 0): everyone gets 50%. Learning from student 1 (failed) moves the weights to (−0.25, −0.25); learning from student 3 (passed) moves them to (0.116, 0.847). After many more steps the model says "pass if you study more than about 2.5 hours".

how.title: Count the kinds of mistakes
how.html: The confusion matrix counts true/false positives and negatives. Accuracy: fraction right overall (misleading if 95% of cases are negative). Precision: of those you flagged, how many were right (matters for spam filters). Recall: of the real positives, how many you caught (matters for disease screening). F1 balances the two.

how.title: Many classes: one neuron per class
how.html: For K classes, use K neurons, each with its own weights (a weight matrix with one column per class). Each produces a score called a logit. Labels are written as one-hot vectors: class 3 of 4 is [0, 0, 1, 0], so no class looks "bigger" than another.

how.title: Softmax shares out the probability
how.html: Softmax exponentiates every logit and divides by the total, so all outputs are positive and add to 1. Bigger logits get disproportionately more. Logits (2.0, 1.0, 0.1) become (66%, 24%, 10%). The loss is again −log(probability of the true class).

how.title: Mini-batches: the practical middle ground
how.html: Update after a small batch (32–256 examples) instead of one or all: less noisy than single examples, much faster than full passes, and ideal for GPUs. With 60,000 images and batches of 128 you make 469 updates per pass through the data (an epoch). Start with 128 or 256.

how.title: Predicting and grading many classes
how.html: To predict, compute the logits, apply softmax, pick the biggest (class 2 at 68.7% in the slides' example). Grade with a K × K confusion matrix, per-class precision and recall, then average: macro (every class counts equally) or weighted (by class size). With 1,000 classes, top-5 accuracy asks whether the right answer is among the five best guesses.

how.title: Tips and debugging
how.html: Standardise features, shuffle every epoch, start with η around 0.1 and batch size 128. Compute softmax stably by subtracting the largest logit first. If the loss is NaN, lower η or fix a log(0). If the model always predicts one class, check class balance and labels. A good sanity check: the model should score 100% on a tiny dataset.

demo.html: Press Step twice: you get the slides' two SGD updates, ending at w = (0.116, 0.847). Notice the two failing students' predictions actually go up at first. Keep pressing Play or Run 1 epoch and watch the S-curve sharpen around 2.5 hours as the loss falls.

example.html:
Spam detection, medical diagnosis (binary), handwritten digits and ImageNet (multi-class, 10 and 1,000 classes), news topics and phoneme recognition. The slides' 3-class confusion matrix (45/38/44 correct out of 150) gives 84.7% accuracy.

Supplementary Classifying network alarms into fault types (power, fibre cut, configuration, hardware) from KPI features is a softmax problem; because some fault types are rare, report per-class recall and macro-F1, not just accuracy.

misunderstandings: Logistic regression is a regression method.
It's a classifier; it models the log-odds as a linear function.
You must always use 0.5 as the threshold.
0.5 is the default; move it to trade precision for recall.
90% accuracy means the classifier is good.
With imbalanced classes a do-nothing model can score that; look at recall, precision and the confusion matrix.
With two classes, softmax reduces exactly to a sigmoid of the logit difference.
They give smoother gradients but fewer updates per epoch and can generalise worse.
takeaways: Logistic regression = linear score + sigmoid → P(class 1); predict 1 when wᵀx ≥ 0.
Train with cross-entropy; its gradient is simply (ŷ − y)·x.
SGD updates per example; mini-batch SGD (B ≈ 32–256) is the practical standard.
Multi-class: K logits Z = XW, softmax to probabilities, categorical cross-entropy; gradient Xᵀ(Ŷ − Y)/B.
Evaluate with the confusion matrix, precision, recall, F1 (per class, macro/weighted) and top-k.
thirty: A linear classifier computes a weighted sum of the features. For two classes, logistic regression passes it through a sigmoid to get the probability of the positive class, and predicts positive when the sum is at least zero, so the decision boundary is a hyperplane. It's trained with cross-entropy, whose gradient is just prediction minus label times the input, usually with stochastic or mini-batch gradient descent. For K classes we use K output neurons, turn their logits into a probability distribution with softmax, and minimise categorical cross-entropy. We evaluate with a confusion matrix, precision, recall and F1, macro or weighted averages, and top-k accuracy when there are many classes.
